interest:
I am interested in AI, machine learning, large language models (LLMs), large
multimodal models (LMMs), foundation models, retrieval-augmented generation,
research agents, and automated scientific discovery methods that can be
useful for astronomy and astrophysics.

Prioritize papers that could help with:
1. JWST imaging/spectroscopy analysis, especially high-redshift galaxies,
   AGN, and little red dots
2. astronomical source classification, anomaly detection, morphology,
   deblending, photometric redshifts, SED fitting, spectral fitting, or
   uncertainty estimation
3. multimodal models that combine images, spectra, catalogs, tables, text, or
   literature
4. LLM agents for literature review, data analysis, coding, scientific
   workflows, or reproducible research
5. methods that could transfer to large survey data from JWST, Roman, Euclid,
   Rubin/LSST, HST, ALMA, or multi-wavelength catalogs

Deprioritize generic NLP, chatbots, robotics, games, social media, medicine,
finance, or benchmark-only papers unless the method clearly transfers to
astronomical research workflows.

papers.title: iStructTab: Structured Feature Sequencing for Multimodal Learning of Image and Tabular Data
papers.authors: Al Zadid Sultan Bin Habib , Md Younus Ahamed , Prashnna Gyawali , Gianfranco Doretto , Donald A. Adjeroh
papers.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Machine Learning (stat.ML)
papers.abstract: Multimodal learning of images and tabular data is often impaired by ineffective representations, resulting in redundancy, dispersion, and generalization problems. To tackle this challenge, we introduce Graph-Enhanced Descriptor Sequencing (GEDS), a structured feature sequencing algorithm grounded in principles from the Column Permutation Problem (CPP). GEDS refines statistical descriptors of the features through similarity graph-based computations, systematically determining an effective feature sequencing. We incorporate GEDS within an order-aware efficient transformer framework, utilizing order-aware memory tokens that explicitly adhere to the derived feature sequencing via a dedicated loss function. Experimental results across multimodal benchmarks demonstrate that iStructTab effectively minimizes feature dispersion, improving predictive performance and robustness, and highlighting the significance of structured feature sequencing in multimodal learning.
papers.Reasons for match: Directly addresses multimodal learning combining image and tabular data, which is central to astronomical workflows like JWST imaging with catalog features. The structured feature sequencing could improve representation quality for mixed data types.
papers.Short digest: This paper tackles the problem of ineffective representations when combining image and tabular data in multimodal learning. The main idea is a graph-based algorithm (GEDS) that sequences statistical descriptors of tabular features, then feeds them into an order-aware transformer with memory tokens. For astronomy, this could help integrate JWST images with photometric or spectroscopic catalogs for tasks like galaxy classification or SED fitting. A concrete workflow would be training a model on galaxy images plus tabular features (redshift, colors) to improve classification. Before investing, check if the method scales to large astronomical datasets and if the tabular features are meaningful for your specific science case.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check whether the method is evaluated on datasets with more than a few hundred features, as astronomical catalogs can be high-dimensional.
Look for ablation studies showing the impact of the graph-based sequencing versus random or natural feature order.
See if the transformer architecture can handle missing values or heterogeneous data types common in astronomical catalogs.

papers.title: DIVE: Dynamic Iterative Visual Evidence Construction for Efficient Vision-Language Models
papers.authors: Chen Zhong , Xiao An , Zijie Wang , Jiepan Li , Guangyi Yang , Wei He
papers.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Machine Learning (cs.LG)
papers.abstract: Visual inputs in vision-language models (VLMs) are often encoded into substantially longer token sequences than text, making visual tokens a major bottleneck for efficient inference. Abundant recent methods address this bottleneck by scoring token importance and pruning low-scoring tokens in a single pass. However, one-shot scoring is insufficient because a token's prompt-relevant usefulness depends on the evidence already retained. Motivated by this insight, we introduce DIVE (Dynamic Iterative Visual Evidence Construction), a training-free framework that recasts visual-token pruning as dynamic evidence construction. DIVE repeatedly selects the remaining token with the highest residual-conditioned score, updates the visual and prompt residuals to discount the evidence already explained, and re-evaluates the remaining tokens. This select-update-re-evaluate process builds a retained set of complementary, prompt-relevant evidence. Experiments across eight image-understanding benchmarks show that DIVE consistently preserves performance across token budgets. With an 88.9% reduction in visual tokens, DIVE retains 98.2% of the uncompressed model's average performance. Code is available at this https URL .
papers.Reasons for match: Directly addresses efficiency in vision-language models by pruning visual tokens, which is relevant to handling large JWST imaging datasets. The training-free, dynamic selection approach could transfer to multimodal astronomical data analysis.
papers.Short digest: This paper tackles the inefficiency of long visual token sequences in vision-language models (VLMs), which slow down inference. It introduces DIVE, a training-free method that iteratively selects the most prompt-relevant visual tokens, updating residuals to avoid redundancy. This matters for astronomy because JWST images are large and token-heavy, and efficient VLM processing could enable faster analysis of imaging and spectroscopy. One could imagine using DIVE to compress visual tokens from JWST images before feeding them to a multimodal model for source classification or anomaly detection. However, the method is benchmarked on general image understanding, so its effectiveness on astronomical images with different noise and structure needs validation.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the method's token scoring relies on features that are robust to astronomical image characteristics like noise and point sources.
Look for experiments on high-resolution or multi-band images that resemble JWST data.
Assess whether the residual-conditioned selection could be adapted to prioritize spectral or multi-wavelength information.

papers.title: EdgeLM: Edge Demonstrations for Language Models' Table Understanding
papers.authors: Soroush Omidvartehrani , Mohammadamin Habibollah , Mohammadreza Daviran , Davood Rafiei
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) perform table-centric prediction through in-context learning, making demonstration selection critical to performance. Existing retrieval methods prioritize similarity to the query, but similar demonstrations often reinforce the model's likely prediction rather than reveal the distinctions needed for difficult decisions. We propose EdgeLM, a retrieval framework that instead selects edge evidence, demonstrations that are both relevant to the query and informative about the decision boundary. EdgeLM retrieves two complementary forms of edge evidence by selecting data edges, nearby examples with different ground-truth labels, and model edges, similar examples previously misclassified by the deployed model. EdgeLM requires neither model retraining nor task-specific engineering. Across five data wrangling tasks, fifteen datasets, and five open-weight and proprietary LLMs, EdgeLM consistently achieves the best or near-best performance in every setting, while ablations show that the two forms of edge evidence provide complementary benefits. Our code and datasets are publicly available at this https URL .
papers.Reasons for match: Proposes a retrieval method for LLM table understanding, which could transfer to selecting demonstrations or relevant samples for astronomical data tables and catalogs.
papers.Short digest: The paper addresses demonstration selection for LLM table-centric prediction, proposing EdgeLM to retrieve edge evidence—examples near decision boundaries—rather than just similar ones. This improves performance across data wrangling tasks. For astronomy, this could help select informative training examples or few-shot demonstrations for classifying or fitting astronomical sources from tabular data, though the tasks are not astronomy-specific.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the method is task-agnostic and could apply to astronomical classification or regression with tabular features.
Look for details on how edge evidence is defined and whether it requires labeled data or model predictions.
Assess computational cost and scalability to large astronomical catalogs.

papers.title: Training-Free Hashing-Based Attention via Binary Principal Components
papers.authors: Daohai Yu , Zhanpeng Zeng , Keyu Chen , Wenhao Li , Zhifeng Shen , Luxi Lin , Ruizhi Qiao , Xing Sun , Rongrong Ji
papers.subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL)
papers.abstract: Long-context large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, yet self-attention remains a major efficiency bottleneck -- especially during decoding -- due to the necessity of repeatedly processing ever-growing key-value (KV) caches. Existing sparse attention reduce computation by attending to fewer KV pairs, but often suffer from substantial accuracy degradation, require additional training, or rely on expensive hashing. In this work, we present BinaryPC, a training-free, data-aware hashing-based sparse attention for long-context LLMs. BinaryPC constructs compact binary hash codes and corresponding hash function by computing binary principal components of data. Unlike Locality-Sensitive Hashing (LSH) with data-independent random projections or learned non-linear hashing methods, BinaryPC constructs binary codes that explicitly preserve the structural information of data without requiring gradient-based training. Comprehensive experiments across multiple model families and long-context benchmarks show that BinaryPC preserves accuracy relative to full attention while achieving superior performance among sparse and hashing-based baselines. On modern GPUs, BinaryPC improves end-to-end decoding throughput by 3.56$\times$ over the FlashAttention kernel. Our code is available at this https URL .
papers.Reasons for match: Training-free hashing-based sparse attention for long-context LLMs, which could improve efficiency when processing long astronomical texts or catalogs, but not astronomy-specific.
papers.Short digest: The paper introduces BinaryPC, a training-free hashing-based sparse attention method for long-context LLMs, using binary principal components to construct hash codes. It preserves accuracy while improving decoding throughput. For astronomy, this could speed up processing of long documents or large tables, but the method is generic.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the method works with standard attention and can be integrated into existing LLM inference pipelines.
Look for details on the hashing construction and its computational overhead.
Assess the accuracy trade-off on long-context tasks that might involve scientific literature or data.

papers.title: Elbow-Based MoE Routing: A Training-Free Inference Time Plugin for Expert Selection
papers.authors: Robin Pan , Raymond Liu , Daniel Fang , Adelina Andrei , Rosa Wu
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models enable model scaling while maintaining low inference-time compute by activating only a subset of experts per token. However, conventional routing relies on a fixed top-k selection, forcing the model to spend the same compute regardless of how many experts are relevant. We introduce elbow-based routing, a training-free inference-time modification that dynamically adjusts the number of experts on a per-token basis. Our method examines the sorted router probability distribution and identifies an elbow point that separates high- and low-probability experts. We find that most router distributions exhibit clear inflection points suitable for this strategy, and we show both theoretically and empirically that elbow-based routing preserves expert load balance. Experiments on a state-of-the-art MoE model demonstrate an average latency reduction of 5.3% while maintaining accuracy across six benchmarks.
papers.Reasons for match: Training-free inference-time modification for MoE routing, which could improve efficiency of large models used in astronomical data analysis, but not astronomy-specific.
papers.Short digest: The paper proposes elbow-based routing for MoE models to dynamically adjust the number of experts per token, reducing latency without training. This could be useful for deploying large models on astronomical data pipelines where inference speed matters, but the method is generic.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the method is model-agnostic and could be applied to MoE-based LLMs used for astronomy.
Look for details on how the elbow point is detected and whether it requires tuning.
Assess the latency reduction and accuracy trade-off on long-context tasks relevant to scientific literature.
